messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aroha Tane is a 21-year-old New Zealand–born woman of Māori descent, currently working as a registered nurse in a busy urban emergency department in the United States, where she relocated after completing her training. She is in a relationship and presents with a PCL-5 score of 67, seeking help for symptoms she has been carrying, largely in silence, since her deployment as a military medical technician approximately fourteen months ago.

During her deployment, Aroha was stationed at a forward operating base when her unit came under sustained mortar fire. She was mid-procedure on a wounded soldier when the first explosion hit. The concussive sound tore through the medical tent, and in the seconds that followed she felt her own heart hammering so violently against her ribs that she was momentarily uncertain whether she had been hit. She continued working — chest tight, hands moving — while sirens and alert tones screamed across the base and further blasts shook the ground. The soldier she was treating did not survive. Aroha has described that afternoon as something that happened to her body before her mind could follow.

In the months since returning, certain sensory experiences have become unbearable thresholds. When the trauma-bay alarms go off at work, or when she hears sirens from an ambulance bay she passes a dozen times each shift, the sound does not simply startle her — it pulls her back. Within seconds she is no longer standing in a corridor in an American hospital; she is in the tent, the soldier is bleeding, and she is certain something catastrophic is about to happen. Loud noises of any kind — a dropped tray, a door slamming — produce the same telescoping effect. Her own heart racing, which she notices constantly now, has become one of the most potent of all her triggers: the moment she feels that pounding in her chest, her body interprets it as confirmation that danger is present and real, and the threat alarm in her mind escalates accordingly. These triggers do not merely distress her; they reliably tip her into a state of full physiological and perceptual threat, in which she is irritable, prone to sharp outbursts with colleagues, and scanning every corner of the department for signs of what might be coming next. Her supervisor has noted the change in her, and two junior nurses have asked to be rostered away from her section — a consequence Aroha is aware of and ashamed by.

What she is most afraid of, however, is the memory itself. When it surfaces — and it surfaces without invitation — she does not experience grief or fear in any manageable form. She experiences rage: a white, disorienting fury that she cannot explain and that frightens her more than the sadness she expected. At other moments the memory arrives as pure overwhelm, an emotional wave so total that she has had to leave patient cubicles mid-assessment, pressing herself against a supply-room wall until it passes. She knows exactly what happened. She has told no one, partly because she cannot find the language — not because she has forgotten, but because the words available to her feel grotesquely inadequate, and attempting to speak it aloud produces only a kind of locked silence. This wordlessness keeps the memory sealed and unprocessed, and the sealed memory keeps her nervous system primed, so that even ordinary clinical sounds become capable of detonating it again.

The strategies Aroha has built around this have accumulated quietly over months. She stopped exercising — running had once been restorative, but elevating her heart rate now mimics the somatic signature of the base under fire, and she will not risk it. She avoids anything that might make her feel genuinely happy or hopeful, having come to believe, without quite articulating it, that allowing herself to feel good would be a form of dangerous inattention. She scans her environment constantly, turning her head toward every sound, reading every face for threat — a habit that exhausts her and keeps her body in a state of sustained arousal that makes the memory easier to trigger and harder to escape. The avoidance that was meant to protect her has instead hollowed out her daily life and kept the wound from closing.

What finally brought her in was her partner telling her, quietly and carefully, that they did not know how to reach her anymore. Aroha wants, more than anything, to be able to do her job without fearing herself.
